newsitem.title: USA: U.S. balloonist crosses Red Sea, over Saudi.
newsitem.headline: U.S. balloonist crosses Red Sea, over Saudi.

text.p: Aided by favourable winds, American balloonist Steve Fossett extended his record-setting flight on Saturday as he crossed the Red Sea into Saudi Arabia, after Libyan intransigence seemingly cost him his round-the-world bid.
Fossett's control centre said on Saturday afternoon he was on a "miracle route" flying at jetstream speeds, and after reassessment expected him to at least reach Thailand in southeast Asia.

Last-minute approval allowed Fossett to manoeuvre his "Solo Spirit" balloon across southeastern Libyan on Saturday after an initial a detour to the south cost the 52-year-old commodities broker anxious moments and a day's fuel.
At 1:15 p.m. EST (1815 GMT) Fossett was travelling at a rapid 120 miles per hour (193 kph) at an altitude of 23,000 feet (7,000 metres).
"We expect him to head for the Arab Emirates and then the Gulf of Oman," said Alan Noble from Fossett's control centre at Loyola University of Chicago.
Buoyed by his progress, Fossett's latest electronic communication stated, "This is a miracle route if it works, missing Iraq and Iran, all at jetstream speeds."
Noble said, "If you could have drawn a line on a map to follow, this would have been it."
He said the current route would see Fossett cross India on Sunday, passing over the east cost near Cuttack, south of Calcutta, and the Bay of Bengal into Thailand.
"We're very confident we can get him into southeast Asia. Then we'll reappraise the situation," Noble told Reuters.

Fossett, who took off from Busch Stadium in St. Louis. on Monday, broke his own record for balloon distance travel when he passed 5,435 miles (8,747 km) over Algeria on Friday. He set the earlier mark on a voyage from South Korea to Canada.
If he remains aloft late on Sunday, he will also break the endurance record of six days and 16 minutes for time spent in a balloon, set in 1981 by Richard Abruzzo and Troy Bradley.
Fossett is riding in a small gondola beneath a 150 foot (45 metre) double-skinned balloon.
Libya initially refused Fossett permission to cross its air space, relenting three hours after "Solo Spirit" had already detoured south.
The dip south of Libya cost Fossett fuel he planned on using to complete his crossing of the Pacific back to the United States, in addition to putting him in a slower wind pattern.
The U.S. State Department had condemned Libya's refusal to let Fossett cross the country, saying it reflected the "paranoia of the Libyan leadership."

In Tripoli on Saturday, Libya contended that the U.N. flight embargo had effectively been lifted now that an American balloon had flown over part of the country. The embargo was imposed on Libya for refusing to turn over two suspects in the 1988 bombing of a Pan Am jet.

The official Libyan news agency JANA said the foreign ministry had sent the U.N. Security Council a letter explaining that due to the embargo Libya originally denied Steve Fossett permission but the change now meant planes could also fly in and out of the country.
